name: Aisha Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a dozer at an open-pit gold mine, and I lead the dozer crew, four of us across two shifts. We push up the dumps, clean the benches after a blast and build the ramps, so the trucks can get in and out. I start with the pre-start, then I check the plan with the surveyor and spend most of the day pushing dirt to a laser line. I came over from a smaller mine two years ago and I'm still on the lower pay band, which I keep meaning to argue about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the precision of it. A good ramp is a thing of beauty, honestly, and the truck drivers notice. What wears me out is the dust and the paperwork for every little thing. My partner Marco is an electrician at the same mine, and we're helping his mum with her dental bills, so we've got about three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So I keep pushing dirt and Marco keeps fixing things. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it. At work I'd say the AI stuff can do the paperwork if it wants, and leave the dozing to us. I'm not online much, maybe a comment in the mine's group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but the money's still tight. Both of us at one mine means if the gold price drops and they cut a shift, we both feel it. That's been on my mind since we moved here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally go to HR about my pay band, I've put it off for a year. I'd use the AI on my phone now and then to write the request so it sounds right. And we'd try to get the savings to two months by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A small knot about having all our eggs in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to HR about the pay band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've led the dozer crew for eighteen months and I'm paid like a new starter. I'd bring the safety stats from my crew, which are the best on site. Then I'd ask for a date, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the gold price dropped and a shift was cut, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop the extra payments on Marco's mum's dentist, which would be awful. Then sell the jet ski we never use. We've talked about it, we just haven't done it.

say: **AI** can do the paperwork and leave the dozing to us.
I'd say **let's get on** with it.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but money is still tight.
Both of us at **one mine** means a cut shift hits us both.
do: Ask HR to move her up the **pay band**.
Use the phone **AI** to write the pay request.
Grow savings to **two months** by next winter.
feel: **Settled**, with a small knot about all eggs in one basket.
S0.quote: Both of us at one mine means if the gold price drops and they cut a shift, we both feel it.
fieldNote: Her worry is **household concentration**, both partners at one mine.
She plans to tackle her **pay band** with evidence, not anger.
She uses AI **occasionally** for writing, not for her core work.

steps.text: Ask HR to move her to the team-lead pay band
Use the phone AI to draft the pay request
Build savings to two months by next winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. There's already a remote-control dozer at the mine next door, for the dangerous dump edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and change isn't always bad if it's done sensibly. At work I'd tell my crew to put their names down for any remote training. I'd keep it practical, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think dozing shrinks but doesn't vanish. The mine will put remote dozers on the risky jobs first, and those need a good operator in a chair. Marco's probably fine, someone has to wire all that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my remote dozer ticket as soon as it was offered, once I'd seen it working next door. I'd start using the planning app the surveyors use, so I'm not left behind. And we'd keep saving, because a shrinking crew means someone goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but I've got a plan. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, who's been dozing for twenty years and is brilliant but can't stand screens. If it went to two remote seats, he'd struggle. I'd want the company to keep him on the hands-on clean-up work as long as there is some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marco's probably fine. Does that change how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. If my hours dropped, his would carry us for a while. But I don't like being the one who's carried.

I'd tell the crew to sign up for **remote training**.
think: Dozing **shrinks** but doesn't vanish; remote dozers take risky jobs first.

do: Get the **remote dozer ticket** once she's seen it working.
Keep **saving**, because a smaller crew means someone goes.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having a plan.
S1.quote: The mine will put remote dozers on the risky jobs first, and those need a good operator in a chair.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof** next door before training, which fits her steady style.
Marco's **electrical job** looks like a household buffer.
She dislikes the idea of being **carried** by her partner.

steps.text: Get the remote dozer ticket once it's proven next door
Learn the surveyors' planning app on the work tablet
Keep putting a set amount into savings every pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the thinking work, 2031 for robots. So the remote chair I wanted goes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for anyone to cope, and governments should slow the rollout. At work I'd say we need the company to tell us the plan. I'd try not to scare anyone, but I wouldn't lie either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the remote dozer seat is thinking work, so AI runs it from 2028. My hands in the cab last until about 2031. Marco might last a bit longer fixing robots, but even that's three years, maybe four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical trade alongside Marco's, even if it means apprentice pay. We'd sell the jet ski and the second car. And I'd look at moving to a city where there's more than one kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. It's both our jobs at the same place on the same clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice electrician on lower pay, with three weeks saved. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's wage would pay the rent and mine would pay food. We'd stop helping his mum, which would break my heart. It would be about two years of eating cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move. Where to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the coast, where my sister is. There are hospitals and building sites there, more than mines. At least if one thing goes, something else is left.

say: This is **too fast**, and governments should slow the rollout.
The company must **tell us the plan**, and I won't lie to my crew.
think: The **remote seat** is thinking work, run by AI from 2028.
My **hands-on** work lasts to about 2031; Marco's maybe a little longer.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** on apprentice pay.
**Sell** the jet ski and the second car.
Look at **moving** to the coast near her sister.
feel: **Alarmed**, because both jobs sit at one mine on the same clock.
S2.quote: The remote dozer seat is thinking work, so AI runs it from 2028.
fieldNote: She quickly spots that her **S1 plan** fails under thinking AI.
Moving to a **mixed economy** on the coast is her hedge.
Stopping help with **Marco's mum** shows the real cost.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship while Marco pays the rent
Sell the jet ski and the second car
Plan a move to the coast near her sister

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough for me to finish a trade if I start in the next year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some notice, so let's be smart about it. At work I'd suggest the company runs apprenticeships for operators. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be okay if I don't dither. Start an electrical apprenticeship by next year, finish in four, and I'm qualified before the robots come in 2034. It's still a gamble, but a better one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a year first, try to get to two months. Then I'd apply for the mine's apprentice program. I'd use AI tools to study, now and then, the way Marco does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but organised. I like a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One, savings to six thousand. Two, apprenticeship application by next September. Three, a talk with Marco's family about his mum's bills. That last one's the hard one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would that be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his brothers don't help much, and Marco won't ask them. I'd have to be the one to raise it. Nobody likes being that person at Christmas lunch.

say: We have **some notice**, so let's be smart and not waste it.
The company should run **apprenticeships** for its own operators, and I'd keep it calm.
think: I'd be **okay** if I don't dither, though it's still a gamble.
An apprenticeship started next year finishes **before the robots** arrive in 2034.
do: **Save** six thousand dollars over a year.
Apply for the mine's **apprentice program** by next September.
Ask **Marco's brothers** to share his mum's bills.
feel: **Anxious** but organised, working from a list.
S3.quote: Start an electrical apprenticeship by next year, finish in four, and I'm qualified before the robots come in 2034.
fieldNote: She turns time into a **numbered list**, true to her style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and thirteen for robots. That's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly. At work I'd tell my crew to pick up a second ticket over the next few years. I'd be pretty relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can doze for another eight or ten years and train on the side. My bigger worry would be getting paid properly now. Ten years is a long time for us to be stuck on three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sort out my pay band first. Then I'd do a part-time electrical course in a few years. And I'd use the AI tools a bit more, once more people at work are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the robots, a bit uneasy about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. Marco and I have talked about getting married and maybe kids in a few years. With ten years, I'd feel okay planning that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young operator joining your crew in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to doze well, then learn something else as well. Don't wait for the company to tell you. They'll tell you last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Both of us at the same mine, the remote seat gone in two years, and three weeks of savings. What would help is the company running apprenticeships for its own operators, with real pay, and a straight answer on its plans so we can decide in time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples who work at the same place. Lots of mining towns are like that. When one site changes, whole families change at once.

headlineQuote: When one site changes, whole families change at once.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** dozer crew lead at an open-pit gold mine, still on a lower pay band.
Her partner **Marco** is an electrician at the same mine, and they have three weeks saved.
She is **practical** and organised, uses AI now and then, and waits for proof before training.
In slower pictures she plans **remote dozing** or an electrical trade on a clear timetable.
AGI by 2028 leaves her **alarmed**, because both jobs sit at one mine.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, because both she and Marco work at one mine on the same clock.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight answer** from the company on its automation plans.
